title: Dental minister fails to confirm contract reform within Labour’s term
html:
When asked whether the government’s pledge to reform the NHS dental contract by the end of this Parliamentary term would be delivered, dental minister James Frith failed to provide the reassuring and simple yes that the industry has been crying out for.

‘We are committed to improving access to National Health Service dentistry, and reforming the dental contract is a key part of this, alongside boosting the numbers of dentists delivering NHS work, using technology to improve services, and ensuring we are doing everything we can to prevent poor oral health,’ he said in response to the question by Green Party MP Adrian Ramsay.

‘We will provide further details on our plans in this area, including any consultation exercises, in due course.’

In March, the government pledged ‘to fundamentally reform the dental contract by the end of this Parliament’. The next general election must take place by August 2029.

British Dental Association (BDA) chair Eddie Crouch has been a vocal critic of the lack of details. Responding to health secretary Yvette Cooper’s Labour Party conference speech, which gave only a passing mention to dentistry, he said the lack of clarity ‘gives little hope to a demoralised profession or the millions struggling to access care’

Frith was, however, able to verify that data relating to the number of complex care pathways which have been opened since June 2026 would be published as part of the dentistry annual statistics in the summer of 2027.

He also noted that three clinical advisors appointed in 2024 to give advice on dentistry were no longer employed as of November 2026, with no plans to replace them. Frith said that the chief dental officer (CDO) for England, Jason Wong, remains the principal dental advisor to department of health and social care.

What has the government said about dental contract reform so far?

In recent discussions on the topic of NHS dentistry, Frith has reiterated Labour’s previous changes such as the introduction of an NHS tie-in for dental graduates and the allocation of 50 new dental school places.

But with social care at the centre of the government’s health agenda, budget, time and interest may all be barriers to delivering fundamental dental contract reform.

In October, a survey sent to all 650 MPs on the topic of NHS dentistry received just 12 replies. All 12 agreed that the NHS dental contract needed to change, with eight giving the availability of NHS dentistry in their constituencies the lowest possible score.

Frith is due to speak at the General Dental Council’s Dental Leadership Network event on Tuesday November 24th,
